title: 800 Attributes to the Few That Mattered
impact: 30% conversion lift; $150K saved (text mining); $400K / 15% op-cost cut; $360K account salvaged and upsized
earned_secret: The model was never the hard part. With 800 attributes, the lever was ruthless subtraction to the few variables that actually moved conversion, and translating a fuzzy business goal into something measurable. Most people reach for more, more features, bigger models. The value was in cutting. That same subtraction instinct is how I run AI systems now: deciding what not to build and what not to automate.

title: Offline Attribution Pipeline
impact: Net-new offline-attribution capability; $100K deal closed; productized as a reusable client-portal report
earned_secret: I don't solve for one client, I productize the solve so it compounds. Turning a bespoke attribution request into a reusable portal capability is what turned a single $100K deal into a repeatable product line.

title: Inventory Quality System, Fraud Detection 0-to-1
impact: ~$3.75M incremental + $250K annual savings (~$4M aggregate, the resume figure); 20% partner-margin lift
earned_secret: External vendors gave a binary fraud flag; the internal model gave a continuous, tunable per-partner score. That tunability, plus setting the block threshold where false-block cost exceeds fraud damage, is what made it worth building. That is the same precision/recall threshold judgment I apply to AI guardrails now.

title: Bid-Propensity Traffic Filtering, Bid Prediction ML
impact: $1.2M incremental revenue (LOCKED Aug 18 2026, confirmed defensible, on resume v3); higher bid density
earned_secret: More traffic looks like more opportunity; it is the opposite. Undifferentiated volume depresses bid rates and pushes partners to throttle, so the yield lever was smarter traffic, not bigger. And the refresh cadence was a product decision, not a technical one: weekly caught drift without over-correcting on noise.

title: APM Team Development, Team Leadership
impact: 4 APMs developed into independent vertical owners; 6 solution engineers coached to product thinking
earned_secret: I taught engineers to judge when a partner request needs custom eng, when it can be templated, and when it should become a scalable pipeline. That build-vs-scale judgment is what turns an order-taker into a product owner, and ownership follows accountability (OKR-linked), not instruction.

title: Publisher Diagnostics Platform, 0-to-1 to Productionised
impact: $1.3M combined ($567K ops hours saved across 26 members, $600K demand-tag performance post ads.txt, $200K fill-rate lift); 35% ticket reduction; 2,500+ tags monitored; Ops runs supply business independently
earned_secret: I filtered every feature request through one question, does this reduce manual effort at scale or solve a one-off? That discipline is what kept the platform from becoming a feature graveyard. And the phasing was the judgment, not the build: ship functional under constraints in Phase 1, then use the promotion mandate to productionise properly in Phase 2.

title: Native Enablement via Programmatic, First TV OEM
impact: First TV OEM to enable programmatic across all ad formats; $16M annual revenue (predominantly incremental) in ~1.5 yrs; home-screen fill 25% -> monetized; DV360, Yahoo, TTD + Magnite/ClearLine + 7 resellers on S2S
earned_secret: I didn't wait for demand to be proven before building. I proposed building the infrastructure in parallel with beta clients because the timing was the asset, not the certainty. And in the waterfall, managed demand wins over programmatic: you protect the pre-committed revenue while you prove the new business, you don't cannibalize before it's proven.

title: Alt ID Infrastructure, Contrarian Bet
impact: UID2, RampID, ConnectID, Epsilon, Pair, Viant, ID5 across US/CA/EU5 + Google PAL & Amazon APS globally; 60% O&O CTV coverage; 3X bid rates; $3M+ incremental annual revenue
earned_secret: The gap was the signal. LG wasn't even having the identity conversation the rest of the room was having, and recognizing an absence as an opportunity before there's internal appetite is the contrarian bet. On execution: buy for speed where you're behind (bought IP-to-HEM mapping for immediate coverage), but build where lock-in would cost you leverage (built the ingestion layer so we could onboard any ID partner on our terms).

title: GDPR Compliance & EU Revenue Protection
impact: $6M EU programmatic revenue retained; 60%+ opt-in (vs 55% target, near UK's 65%); $2M managed loss within projection, offset by programmatic growth; net EU revenue positive; LG Ads established as fully GDPR-compliant programmatic partner
earned_secret: Sales didn't need convincing that compliance was right, they needed to see non-compliance was more expensive. The $2M-vs-$4M asymmetry unlocked everything. That's the difference between a product leader and a policy enforcer: you speak in the language of the room you're in.

title: OOH & Inventory Expansion, Ambiguity & Guardrails
impact: Killed a legally-blocked in-vehicle integration (saved eng); blocked sound-on-by-default across new formats (protected home-screen trust); 100% hotel inventory consolidation ($100K live, $1.8M projected at scale, $2M on contract); intake framework became the LG-HQ operating model
earned_secret: The win wasn't any single integration, it was institutionalizing the intake framework so ambiguous LGE requests got evaluated consistently, and it became HQ's operating model. The durable outcome of ambiguity work is the process, not the deal. And on values: partial inventory with split ownership can't become a scalable product, so 100% consolidation was a hard requirement, even at the cost of a month-long negotiation.

title: Adtech Team Turnaround, Structure from Chaos
impact: Turned a 17-person team in permanent fire-drill mode into a roadmap-driven org in ~6 months; analysts could finally choose a product vs engineering track; MVPs started getting productionised instead of piling up
earned_secret: A team drowning in urgent work doesn't need more hands, it needs a filter and a roadmap. I had zero authority over 17 people, so I led two ways: I made every request justify itself with a metric, and I made everyone's impact visible. Once people could see how their work mapped to the business and could choose a track, they self-organized. Authority would have been faster but less durable, they owned the new way of working because they could see why it was better.
